items.title: 9.8 Solubility product (for slightly soluble ionic compounds)

source_refs.note: Topic 9.8 (Solubility Product) with Table 9.5, printed pages 201-202.

blocks.text: When a soluble ionic compound is dissolved in water, like NaCl, it dissociates completely into ions. But for slightly soluble salts the dissociation is not complete at equilibrium stage. For example, when PbSO₄ is shaken with water the solution contains Pb²⁺, SO₄²⁻ and undissociated PbSO₄. It means that equilibrium exists between solid solute, PbSO₄ and the dissolved ions, SO₄²⁻ and SO₄²⁻.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The dissolved ions are Pb²⁺ and SO₄²⁻; the print gives SO₄²⁻ twice.
Lead sulphate is a well-known sparingly soluble compound and it dissociates to a very small extent like PbCl₂.
Being a sparingly soluble salt, the concentration of lead sulphate (PbSO₄) almost remains constant. Bring [PbSO₄] on L.H.S. with Kc.

blocks.text_alt: Kc[PbSO₄] = [Pb²⁺][SO₄²⁻]; if Kc[PbSO₄] = Ksp, then Ksp = [Pb²⁺][SO₄²⁻] = 1.6 × 10⁻⁸ at 25°C

blocks.text: Ksp is called the solubility product of PbSO₄.

blocks.title: Solubility product
blocks.text: It is the product of molar solubilities of two ions at equilibrium stage.
Similarly, for another sparingly soluble salt, PbCl₂.
Ksp is usually a very small quantity at room temperature. The value of Ksp is temperature dependent.

blocks.title: Solubility product (Ksp)
blocks.text: So, the solubility product is the product of the concentrations of ions raised to an exponent equal to the co-efficient of the balanced equation.
The value of Ksp is a measure of the dissociation of sparingly soluble salt.

blocks.text: Three ion products are misprinted: for CuS it is [Cu²⁺][S²⁻], for BaSO₄ [Ba²⁺][SO₄²⁻], and for CaCO₃ [Ca²⁺][CO₃²⁻].
